summary: A German yes/no question puts the conjugated verb first, before the subject: Du trinkst Tee. → Trinkst du Tee? No helper verb is added: the main verb itself moves to the front (Isst er Fleisch? – Does he eat meat?). Everything else keeps its place; a second verb stays at the end (Willst du Tee trinken?). A choice question with oder works the same way (Willst du Tee oder Kaffee?) but is answered with the choice, not with ja or nein. Answers: ja (yes), nein (no) – and doch, the “yes” that contradicts a negative question or statement: Isst du kein Fleisch? – Doch! (Yes, I do.) Small words make questions natural: auch (too: Trinkst du auch Tee?), nur (only), wirklich (really: Isst du wirklich kein Fleisch?) and the replies vielleicht (maybe) and natürlich (of course). In speech the voice usually rises at the end.

blocks.title: doch
blocks.text: doch says “yes” against a negative: Magst du keinen Käse? – Doch! (Yes, I do like it.) Answering ja here would be unclear. Arabic بَلَى (balā) works the same way.

blocks.title: Choice questions with oder
blocks.text: Willst du Tee oder Kaffee? – Kaffee, bitte. The verb is first as in any yes/no question, but the answer is one of the choices. …, oder? at the end of a statement asks for agreement: Das ist gut, oder? (right?).

askYourself: Which verb carries the person ending? Put exactly that verb in first position.
Is the subject a pronoun? It comes straight after the verb (Willst du …?, Trinken Sie …?).
Is there a second verb (an infinitive)? It stays at the end.
Did I add a helper verb? German has none: Isst du …?, not *Tust du essen …?
Is it a choice? → … oder …? – the answer is the choice.
Is the question negative and I want to say yes? → doch.
steps: Move the conjugated verb to the front.
Keep everything else in place; end with a question mark.

traps: No helper verb: the main verb itself moves – Isst du Fleisch? (not *Tust du Fleisch essen?).
The verb form agrees with the subject after it: Willst du …?, Wollen Sie …?, Isst er …?
The second verb does not move: Willst du Tee trinken? (not *Willst trinken du Tee?)
After a negative question, “yes” is doch: Trinkst du keinen Kaffee? – Doch!
A question with oder is not answered with ja / nein.
Statement order with rising intonation (Du trinkst keinen Kaffee?) exists in speech, but it expresses surprise or a check, not a neutral question.

quiz.why: The verb moves to the front; no “do”.

quiz.q: Isst du kein Fleisch? – ___! (Yes, I do.)
Willst du Tee oder Kaffee? – best answer:
quiz.why: A choice question is answered with the choice.
The modal goes first; the infinitive stays at the end.
auch = too; ich auch nicht = me neither.
vielleicht = maybe; natürlich = of course; wirklich = really.

seeAlso.note: Arabic puts هَلْ hal (or أَ ʾa-) before the statement; بَلَى balā is its “doch”.
Hebrew keeps the statement order: intonation (or הַאִם haʾim in writing) makes the question.
Chinese adds 吗 at the end, or uses verb-not-verb (喝不喝), and 还是 for “or” in a choice question.
Negative questions (Isst du kein Fleisch?) are answered with doch or nein.
With a question word (wer, was, wo …) the verb comes second, not first: Was trinkst du?

notes.text: Greek keeps the statement order and changes only the intonation (Πίνεις τσάι;); German moves the verb to the front: Trinkst du Tee? Greek has no single word for doch – it needs a sentence (Ναι, πίνω).
Russian asks by intonation (Ты пьёшь чай?); German must move the verb first: Trinkst du Tee? There is no single word like doch: Russian answers with the verb (Пью!).
Spanish asks by intonation (¿Bebes té?); German moves the verb to the front: Trinkst du Tee?
German adds no do: Do you drink tea? = Trinkst du Tee? (with be, have and modals English inverts as German does). “Yes” to a negative question is doch.
Inversion (Bois-tu du thé ?) is the German pattern, but in German it is the normal question; est-ce que has no counterpart. doch is French si.
Hindi can start with kyā and keeps the verb at the end (kyā tum cāy pīte ho?); German has no question word for yes / no: it moves the verb first.
Persian asks by intonation or with āyā at the start; German moves the verb to the front.
Marathi adds kā at the end (tū cahā pitos kā?); German has no particle: Trinkst du Tee?
Arabic starts with hal or ʾa-; German starts with the verb. balā is exactly doch: “yes” against a negative.
Hebrew asks mostly by intonation (ha-im is formal); German must move the verb first.
Turkish adds the particle mi after the word asked about (Çay içiyor musun?); German has no particle and moves the verb first.
Japanese adds ka at the end (ocha o nomimasu ka?); German moves the verb to the front instead.
Korean asks with the verb ending and intonation (cha masyeoyo?); German moves the verb first.
Finnish also puts the verb first, with -ko / -kö on it (Juotko teetä?); German moves the verb first without any suffix: Trinkst du Tee?
Hungarian asks with a special intonation only (Teát iszol?); German moves the verb to the front.
Swahili may start with Je and otherwise asks by intonation (Je, unakunywa chai?); German moves the verb first.
Chinese adds 吗 (你喝茶吗?) or uses verb-not-verb (你喝不喝茶?); German moves the verb to the front: Trinkst du Tee?
Vietnamese frames the verb with có … không (anh có uống trà không?); German just moves the verb first.
Inuktitut shows a question with a special verb ending (the interrogative mood); German keeps the verb form and moves it to the front.
